strengths: Well-motivated system integration: combining dense learned correspondence estimation (DROID-SLAM style) with visual-inertial preintegration and 3D Gaussian Splatting fills an important gap in making dense radiance-field SLAM robust to motion blur, low texture, and frame drops.

Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation across four diverse benchmark datasets (EuRoC, RPNG AR Table, UTMM, and FAST-LIVO2), demonstrating clear gains in tracking accuracy (ATE) and view synthesis quality (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) against both classic VIO and recent Gaussian SLAM pipelines.

Thoughtful robustness testing via strided frame evaluations (from stride 1 up to stride 40) and extreme condition captures, which convincingly isolates and highlights the tangible benefits of tight IMU fusion under visually degraded regimes.

Efficient loop closure mechanism with analytic batch updates of 3D Gaussian means and covariances under Sim(3) keyframe transforms, avoiding prohibitively expensive map re-optimization upon loop closures.
weaknesses: Moderate conceptual novelty: the system represents primarily an engineering synthesis of established frameworks (DROID-SLAM's ConvGRU BA layer, Forster et al.'s IMU preintegration on manifold, and HI-SLAM2 / Splat-SLAM Gaussian mapping and PGBA).

High computational demand and questionable real-time feasibility on edge devices: Table 9 shows that tracking + mapping runs at ~4–11 FPS (average 7.09 FPS) even on an ultra-high-end NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU, meaning deployment on target AR/VR headsets or robotic platforms remains distant.

Lack of visual-to-map feedback loop: the tracking module operates independently of the synthesized Gaussian radiance field, rendering the 3DGS component strictly a downstream visual reconstruction module rather than an active component in localization/bundle adjustment.

Theoretical ambiguity regarding Sim(3) loop closure in visual-inertial SLAM: because an IMU inherently renders metric scale and gravity direction observable, the choice to optimize relative loop constraints in Sim(3) rather than SE(3) warrants clearer theoretical justification regarding potential conflicts with the metric scale enforced by IMU preintegration.

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation across four diverse benchmarks (EuRoC, RPNG AR Table, UTMM, and FAST-LIVO2), demonstrating competitive tracking accuracy and photorealistic rendering performance compared to both classical VIO and recent 3DGS-SLAM methods.

The robustness analysis under frame subsampling (strided evaluation up to stride=40) and extreme degraded visual conditions is thorough and effectively showcases the value of tightly coupling inertial pre-integration with dense visual representations.
Clear and detailed description of the staged IMU initialization and batch Gaussian transform mechanism during loop closure.
Extensive supplementary material providing per-sequence tracking and novel view synthesis breakdowns, ablation studies, and runtime analyses.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual and algorithmic novelty: the framework is largely an integration of established building blocks—specifically DROID-SLAM's GRU-based correspondence front-end, standard manifold IMU pre-integration (Forster et al.), and Gaussian mapping with pose-graph loop deformation closely following HI-SLAM2.

Asymmetric tracking and mapping coupling: the 3D Gaussian Splatting representation serves strictly as a downstream reconstruction and rendering artifact and does not provide feedback (e.g., photometric tracking or Gaussian-based relocalization) into the tracking front-end.

High computational demand and sub-real-time full system throughput: running tracking and Gaussian mapping achieves only ~7.1 FPS even on top-tier desktop hardware (NVIDIA RTX 5090 and Intel i7-14700K), which presents practical deployment challenges for robotics or mobile AR.

Theoretical ambiguity regarding scale in loop closure: in a visual-inertial system with observable gravity and metric scale, the paper uses Sim(3) pose graph bundle adjustment to correct long-term scale drift rather than an SE(3) formulation, and disables inertial constraints during global BA without sufficient theoretical justification.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical limitation in current dense neural/3DGS SLAM systems, namely that purely visual monocular pipelines easily fail under motion blur, aggressive motion, and textureless environments, whereas visual-inertial fusion can resolve metric scale and stabilize tracking.

The proposed framework tightly integrates learned dense visual correspondences (DROID-style) with IMU pre-integration factors, per-keyframe bias estimation, and a staged initialization scheme that reliably recovers scale and gravity alignment before full joint optimization.

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental validation across four diverse benchmarks (EuRoC, RPNG AR Table, UTMM, and FAST-LIVO2), convincingly demonstrating superior trajectory accuracy (ATE RMSE) and rendering quality against both classic VIO baselines and recent 3DGS SLAM pipelines.

The strided evaluation (simulating large inter-frame motion and frame drops) and extreme-condition test provide strong empirical evidence for the system's robustness compared to purely visual 3DGS methods and sparse feature-based VIO pipelines.
Clear ablation studies validate each major component, including IMU fusion, keyframe initialization, and Gaussian updates during loop closure.
weaknesses: Architectural novelty is somewhat limited: the method largely combines existing modules—DROID-SLAM/HI-SLAM2 learned dense bundle adjustment, standard IMU pre-integration residuals (Forster et al.), and keyframe-anchored 3DGS map deformation upon loop closure—rather than introducing fundamentally new theoretical formulations.

The 3D Gaussian representation acts primarily as a downstream mapping module rather than feeding back into tracking or state estimation; the tracking front-end is effectively a visual-inertial extension of DROID-SLAM, leaving the potential of map-to-frame photometric tracking unexploited.

High computational demand and questionable real-time claim: runtime benchmarks on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 report ~16 FPS for tracking and ~7 FPS for the full tracking-and-mapping pipeline, which is computationally expensive for typical visual-inertial robotics or AR edge platforms.

Potential formulation tension in loop closure: Section 3.1 states that PGBA optimizes in Sim(3) to correct long-term scale drift, yet visual-inertial systems are inherently metric. The manuscript would benefit from clarifying how Sim(3) scale adjustments interact with the gravity vector and metric inertial pre-integration constraints across loops.
